description: We are a team of students interested in science, technology, and space exploration. We enjoy solving problems, working together, and learning new things. We aim to combine our skills and creativity to develop innovative solutions.
summary: In our app, farmers can enter their field’s location and size, what they’ve grown before, their soil measurements, and how many seasons they want to plan for. They can also enter the price of urea if they want to. Farmers can indicate that they plan to sell their crops and get a planting plan tailored to that goal. The app explains why it recommends each choice. In a separate panel, agricultural engineers can enter more detailed soil and crop data, answer additional questions, and get results in a more technical format. The site also shows local climate information, including rainfall and temperature. Our app helps farmers plan productive crop rotations for fields they might otherwise leave fallow. This can help them earn a profit, use less water and fewer resources, and choose crops that make the most productive use of their land.
details:
ARGIS is a project that uses NASA data to make farming smarter and more sustainable. We use NASA POWER for weather and for the soil moisture data used in the planting plan. SMAP shows soil moisture on the map, and MODIS is used to look at plant health.

ARGIS uses the field’s climate, soil conditions, and previous crop to score how suitable different crops are for the field. It then compares different crop rotations based on planting dates, irrigation needs, and whether crops from the same family would be grown back to back. The plan explains why each crop was recommended.

We brought three ideas together in one engine that we call Memory of the Soil, Climate Time Machine, and Crop Recovery. Farmers can find these features in separate tools, but ARGIS combines them in one place using NASA data and other sources like SoilGrids. It uses past data and climate scenarios to show how the field’s history and changes in temperature or rainfall could affect what farmers plant over the next few seasons. Our goal is to help farmers save water, protect their soil, and reduce the risks of choosing a crop that may not grow well in their field.

We designed two views because farmers and agricultural engineers need different levels of detail. In the farmer view, we use everyday language to explain what to plant and why. In the engineer view, users can enter more detailed soil measurements, such as salinity, set irrigation limits, and get more technical results.

We built ARGIS with HTML, CSS, and JavaScript. We used Leaflet for the map, Python to collect and prepare the data, and Node.js, Playwright, and axe for testing.
